To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the seasonal integral of the net exchange of CO2 between the terrestrial biosphere and the atmosphere of the Northern Hemisphere is ∼1.0 Pg C, that the seasonal integral is larger than predicted by models, that the seasonal variation of the integral is smaller than predicted by models and that the seasonal variation is not as large as predicted by models that do not include the effects of the El Nino‐Southern Oscillation.

the Northern Hemisphere growing season NEE, as estimated from column‐averaged CO2 observations, is 25% larger than the NEE estimated by the CASA model and that the bias is caused by too weak vertical diffusion in the transport model.
the CASA model is biased low by ∼25% and that the bias is likely due to a lack of vertical mixing in the model used to infer Northern Hemisphere column‐CO2 from the surface measurements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the estimation of net carbon fluxes in the biosphere, and the role of biospheric carbon fluxes in climate change.
improving the accuracy of our estimates of the annual cycle of Northern Hemisphere NEE, and the seasonal and inter‐annual variability of CO2 fluxes in the terrestrial biosphere.
the development and application of new methods for estimating the net exchange of carbon between the biosphere and the atmosphere.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the growing season net CO2 flux from the land surface to the atmosphere is larger than the CASA model predicts by ∼25%.
the CASA model is a good first approximation for the growing season, but it underestimates the magnitude of NEE by ∼25% in the Northern Hemisphere.
the growing season net flux is 1–2 Pg C yr−1 higher than predicted by CASA, but the uncertainty is still too large to be conclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CASA model is not a good model for NEE in the Northern Hemisphere.

the Northern Hemisphere growing season NEE is larger than previously thought and is ∼1 Pg C more positive than estimated from the CASA model, which is in turn ∼2 Pg C more positive (i.e. less negative) than the model‐inferred NEE from the NOAA‐ESRL flask network.
the Northern Hemisphere growing season NEE is 1.2±0.2 petagram (Pg) of carbon per year, with the uncertainty reflecting the range in NEE values derived from different transport models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the growing season net flux is larger than predicted by CASA.
the seasonal integral of NEE is larger than predicted by models, which is in line with the recent findings of other groups using different methods.
there is a large and significant discrepancy between the observed seasonal cycle of CO2 above the surface and that predicted by CASA.
